blocks.text: A citizen with no party, no money and no soldiers can still stop a government. He files a suit. If the court agrees that his rights were breached, the state must obey — and the only reason that works is an independent judiciary.

blocks.markdown: The **judiciary** is the organ of government that interprets the law and settles disputes according to it. Judicial powers of the Federation and of the states are vested in the courts by section 6 of the 1999 Constitution.

items: **Interpretation of the law** — deciding what a statute or a constitutional provision means when applied to real facts.
**Adjudication** — settling disputes between individuals, between individuals and the state, and between organs and tiers of government.
**Protection of fundamental human rights** — enforcing Chapter IV of the Constitution against government and private persons.
**Judicial review** — declaring void any law or official act that conflicts with the Constitution.
**Punishment of offenders** — trying criminal cases and imposing sentences.
**Guardianship of the Constitution** — ensuring that all organs stay within their constitutional powers.
**Law making through precedent** — decisions of higher courts bind lower courts and so develop the law.
**Advisory and administrative functions** — chairing commissions and tribunals of inquiry, and the Chief Justice's role in constituting an impeachment investigation panel.

rows: Highest and final court; the Chief Justice of Nigeria and not more than 21 Justices; has original jurisdiction in disputes between the Federation and a state, or between states
Headed by the President of the Court of Appeal, with not fewer than 49 Justices; hears appeals from the courts below and, at first instance, presidential election petitions
Federal High Court; High Court of a State; High Court of the Federal Capital Territory; Sharia Court of Appeal; Customary Court of Appeal; National Industrial Court
Superior courts of record with defined subject-matter jurisdiction
Magistrates' and district courts, area courts, customary and sharia courts of first instance
Inferior courts created by state law, handling the bulk of everyday cases

blocks.title: Judicial independence
blocks.text: The freedom of judges to decide cases according to law and evidence alone, without fear or favour from the executive, the legislature, litigants or public opinion. It is the condition on which every other function of the judiciary depends.

blocks.markdown:
### How Nigeria's Constitution protects judicial independence

- **Security of tenure** — a Justice of the Supreme Court or of the Court of Appeal holds office until the age of 70, and other judicial officers until 65; they cannot be dismissed at the pleasure of the executive.
- **A prescribed removal procedure** — removal requires recommendation of the National Judicial Council and, for the most senior offices, an address supported by two-thirds of the Senate.
- **The National Judicial Council** — a body chaired by the Chief Justice that recommends appointments, promotions and discipline, keeping these decisions out of purely political hands.
- **Financial protection** — judicial salaries and the recurrent expenditure of the courts are a first-line charge on the Consolidated Revenue Fund, so they need not be negotiated year by year.
- **Immunity** — judges are not personally liable for acts done in good faith in the exercise of judicial functions.
- **Appointment on merit and professional qualification.**

### Threats to judicial independence

Delay in funding releases, executive disobedience of court orders, corruption and inducement of judicial officers, congestion and long adjournments that ration justice by exhaustion, and — historically under military rule — decrees containing **ouster clauses** that expressly forbade the courts from questioning them.

blocks.title: Choosing the right court
blocks.prompt: Identify the court that should hear each matter: (i) a boundary dispute between Kogi State and Enugu State; (ii) an appeal against a High Court judgment in a land case; (iii) an alleged breach of a citizen's right to personal liberty by the police.

steps.text: (i) A dispute between two states is not an ordinary civil claim. The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction in disputes between states, so it hears the matter first and finally.
(ii) An appeal from a High Court goes to the Court of Appeal, which sits above all the courts in level three of the hierarchy.
(iii) Enforcement of a fundamental right under Chapter IV is brought at first instance before a High Court — the Federal High Court or the High Court of the relevant state or of the FCT.
Note the general rules: original jurisdiction over intergovernmental disputes lies with the Supreme Court, appeals travel upwards one level at a time, and rights enforcement begins in a High Court.

blocks.answer: (i) the Supreme Court in its original jurisdiction; (ii) the Court of Appeal; (iii) a High Court exercising its fundamental rights enforcement jurisdiction

blocks.title: Name the guarantees, not just the ideal
blocks.text: Questions on judicial independence are lost by candidates who only say judges should be free from interference. Name the mechanisms — security of tenure to 70 and 65, removal only through the National Judicial Council and the Senate, salaries as a first-line charge, and judicial immunity. Concrete mechanisms score marks.

points: The judiciary interprets the law, adjudicates disputes, protects fundamental rights and exercises judicial review.
Judicial powers are vested in the courts by section 6 of the 1999 Constitution.
The Supreme Court is the final court and has original jurisdiction in disputes between the Federation and a state or between states.
Below it sit the Court of Appeal, then the Federal and State High Courts, Sharia and Customary Courts of Appeal and the National Industrial Court, then the inferior courts.
Independence is protected by security of tenure, a prescribed removal procedure, the National Judicial Council, salaries as a first-line charge and judicial immunity.
Its main threats are executive interference, funding control, corruption, delay and, historically, ouster clauses in military decrees.
